title: Modulation of physicochemical, textural, rheological, and thermal properties of beeswax oleogels based on the cooling rate and oil phase
content:
Abstract

BACKGROUND

Oleogelation represents a technique used for developing solid fat substitutes from polyunsaturated liquid oils. This study evaluated the effects of canola and, for the first time, peanut and sesame oils, along with three cooling rates applied in oleogel formation (5.5, 7.0, and 10.0 °C min−1), on the modulation of physicochemical, rheological, and thermal stability properties of beeswax oleogels.

RESULTS

The oleogels exhibited acicular crystalline structures, with mean crystal sizes decreasing by over 40% at higher cooling rates, despite the type of oil. X-ray diffraction analysis showed that crystallinity was governed by the beeswax network, with oils acting as fillers in the gelled matrix. Texture parameters such as hardness and adhesiveness increased at higher cooling rates, exhibiting greater resistance to deformation, while springiness and cohesiveness displayed the opposite behavior, indicating better spreadability – properties looked for in solid fat-based food products. Viscoelastic properties exhibit a predominant elastic behavior, with oleogels formed at 10 °C min−1 having higher resistance to deformation and a more robust structure. Complex modulus (G*) showed that thermal stability in oleogels behaves as thixotropic material when submitted to a heating–cooling process; thixotropic index was lower for oleogels formed at 10 °C min−1, suggesting the formation of a stronger network and better thermoreversibility. Thermo-oxidative stability was higher in free oils, whereas oleogels (10 °C min−1) required around 60% more energy (E a) to start oil oxidation.

CONCLUSION

The findings indicate that, even when the type of oil can influence the final characteristics of the oleogel systems, cooling-rate forming conditions play a more significant role in modulating and determining the final properties. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.
